lead: A two-way slab rests on all four edges and has l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> ≤ 2, so it bends in both directions and sends load to all four supports. IS 456 gives its design moments as coefficients times w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>²: Table 26 for panels whose corners are held down (cast with beams or continuous slabs), Table 27 for simply supported panels whose corners can lift. The edge condition, continuous or discontinuous, picks the row. Most room floors in RC framed buildings are two-way slabs.
prereq: You need One-way slabs (effective span, minimum steel, the Ast formula).

sections.h3: How a two-way panel shares its load

blocks.text: Let l<sub>x</sub> be the short effective span and l<sub>y</sub> the long one. Take the two central strips crossing at mid-panel. If both deflect the same, w<sub>x</sub> l<sub>x</sub>⁴ = w<sub>y</sub> l<sub>y</sub>⁴ with w<sub>x</sub> + w<sub>y</sub> = w, so the short span takes w<sub>x</sub> = w l<sub>y</sub>⁴/(l<sub>x</sub>⁴ + l<sub>y</sub>⁴). This is the Rankine–Grashoff split. It ignores the twisting stiffness of the slab, so IS 456 uses coefficients that allow for it, for continuity, and for corners that are held down.

A continuous edge is one where the slab carries on over the beam into the next panel; it has a hogging (negative) moment and needs top steel. A discontinuous edge is the outer edge of the floor or an edge on a wall; the slab is treated as simply supported there. Table 26 lists nine cases: interior panel; one short edge discontinuous; one long edge discontinuous; two adjacent edges discontinuous; two short edges discontinuous; two long edges discontinuous; three edges discontinuous with one long edge continuous; three edges discontinuous with one short edge continuous; four edges discontinuous.
M<sub>x</sub> = α<sub>x</sub> w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>²,   M<sub>y</sub> = α<sub>y</sub> w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>²
blocks.where: Both use l<sub>x</sub>², the short span. α<sub>x</sub> varies with l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> (interpolate between columns); α<sub>y</sub> is one value for each case, in the last column of Table 26. Each case gives a negative coefficient (at continuous edges) and a positive one (mid-span). For Table 27, α<sub>x</sub> = r⁴/(8(1 + r⁴)) and α<sub>y</sub> = r²/(8(1 + r⁴)) with r = l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub>: the Rankine–Grashoff moments.

items: Each direction is split into a middle strip (3/4 of the width) and two edge strips (1/8 each). The table moments apply to the middle strip; edge strips get minimum steel.

Short-span bars go in the outer layer, so d<sub>y</sub> = d<sub>x</sub> − φ. Mid-span bars run to within 0.25l of a continuous edge and 0.15l of a discontinuous edge; top bars over a continuous edge run 0.15l into the span, half of them 0.3l.
At a discontinuous edge, top steel of half the mid-span steel, extending 0.1l, takes care of the partial fixity.

Torsion steel at a corner where both edges are discontinuous: four layers (top and bottom, both ways), each 3/4 of the steel required for the largest mid-span moment, over l<sub>x</sub>/5 from the corner. Half of it where only one edge is continuous; none where both are continuous. Table 27 panels have no torsion steel: their corners are free to lift.

Deflection (cl. 24.1): for l<sub>x</sub> ≤ 3.5 m and live load ≤ 3 kN/m², l<sub>x</sub>/D ≤ 35 (simply supported) or 40 (continuous), times 0.8 for Fe415: 28 and 32. Otherwise check by cl. 23.2 as for one-way slabs.

examples.question: Design a two-way slab for a room 3.4 m × 4.4 m (clear) on 230 mm beams. Two adjacent edges are discontinuous and the corners are held down. Live load 3 kN/m², floor finish 1 kN/m², M20, Fe415, 20 mm cover, 8 mm bars.
steps: Depth: continuous two-way slab, Fe415: l<sub>x</sub>/D ≤ 32, so D ≥ 3496/32 = 109 mm (taking l<sub>x</sub> ≈ 3.5 m). Adopt D = 120 mm; d<sub>x</sub> = 120 − 20 − 4 = 96 mm, d<sub>y</sub> = 96 − 8 = 88 mm.
Spans: l<sub>x</sub> = 3.4 + 0.096 = 3.496 m, l<sub>y</sub> = 4.4 + 0.088 = 4.488 m (both less than centre to centre). l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> = 1.284 ≤ 2: two-way.
Loads: 3.0 + 1.0 + 3.0 = 7.0 kN/m²; w<sub>u</sub> = 10.50 kN/m², and w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>² = 10.50 × 3.496² = 128.33 kN.
Moments (kN·m/m): M<sub>x</sub>(−) = 8.24, M<sub>x</sub>(+) = 6.20, M<sub>y</sub>(−) = 6.03, M<sub>y</sub>(+) = 4.49. The largest is far below M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 1000 × 96² = 25.4 kN·m.

Steel (A<sub>st</sub> formula, then spacing ≤ 3d and 300 mm): M<sub>x</sub>(−) 251 mm² → 8 @ 190 top (265); M<sub>x</sub>(+) 187 → 8 @ 260 bottom (193); M<sub>y</sub>(−) 199 → 8 @ 250 top (201); M<sub>y</sub>(+) 146, raised to the minimum 144 → 8 @ 260 bottom (193).
Edge strips (0.44 m and 0.56 m wide): minimum steel 144 mm²/m, 8 @ 300 mm.

Torsion steel: the corner of the two discontinuous edges needs 0.75 × 187 = 140 mm²/m in each of four layers over 0.70 m × 0.70 m; 8 @ 300 (168 mm²/m) top and bottom both ways. The two corners with one continuous edge need half, 70 mm²/m, also 8 @ 300 (the spacing limit governs).

Shear: V<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> l<sub>x</sub>/2 = 18.35 kN/m (safe: the short span really takes 73 % of the load). τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.191 N/mm²; with p<sub>t</sub> = 0.28 % at the support, kτ<sub>c</sub> = 1.30 × 0.372 = 0.48 N/mm². Safe.
examples.answer: D = 120 mm. Short span: 8 mm @ 260 bottom, 8 mm @ 190 top at the continuous edge. Long span: 8 mm @ 260 bottom, 8 mm @ 250 top at the continuous edge. Torsion mesh 8 mm @ 300 over 0.70 m at the corners.

examples.question: A roof slab 3.5 m × 4.2 m (effective) rests on walls on all four sides; its corners are not held down. w<sub>u</sub> = 10.5 kN/m², d<sub>x</sub> = 96 mm, d<sub>y</sub> = 88 mm. Find M<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>y</sub> and the steel.
steps: A<sub>st</sub>: short span 336 mm²/m (8 mm @ 140), long span 254 mm²/m (8 mm @ 190). No torsion steel.
examples.answer: M<sub>x</sub> = 10.80 and M<sub>y</sub> = 7.59 kN·m/m. The same panel with corners held down and two adjacent edges continuous would have a mid-span M<sub>x</sub> of only 5.79 kN·m/m.

traps: Writing M<sub>y</sub> = α<sub>y</sub> w l<sub>y</sub>². IS 456 uses l<sub>x</sub>² in both directions; with l<sub>y</sub>² the long-span moments of the worked example come out 65 % too large.
Reading the column for l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> but taking α<sub>y</sub> from it too: α<sub>y</sub> is a single value per case, in the last column.
Swapping the layers. Short-span bars go outermost (larger d); d<sub>y</sub> = d<sub>x</sub> − φ.
Giving torsion steel to every corner. Full steel only where both edges are discontinuous, half where one is continuous, none where both are continuous, and none in Table 27 panels.
Using clear spans for l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub>. Use effective spans; the ratio picks the column.

quiz.q: What does a continuous edge mean in Table 26?
quiz.a: An edge where the slab carries on over the support into the next panel, so it has a hogging moment and needs top steel.

quiz.q: How wide are the middle strip and edge strips of a two-way slab?
quiz.a: Middle strip 3/4 of the panel width; each edge strip 1/8.

quiz.q: Why are Table 27 moments larger than Table 26 moments for the same r?
quiz.a: Table 27 panels are simply supported with corners free to lift, so there is no help from continuity or from twisting at held-down corners; all moment is sagging and bigger.

quiz.q: Find the Rankine–Grashoff share of the short span for l<sub>x</sub> = 4 m, l<sub>y</sub> = 5 m.

An interior panel has l<sub>x</sub> = 4.0 m, l<sub>y</sub> = 5.0 m, w<sub>u</sub> = 12 kN/m². Find M<sub>x</sub>(−) and M<sub>y</sub>(+) (Table 26: α<sub>x</sub>(−) at 1.2 = 0.043, at 1.3 = 0.047; α<sub>y</sub>(+) = 0.024).
A designer gives a two-adjacent-edges panel no torsion steel. What happens at the outer corner?
quiz.a: The corner tries to lift and twist; diagonal cracks open on top near the corner and on the bottom across it. The 3/4 mesh in four layers over l<sub>x</sub>/5 controls them.

quiz.q: A panel 3.6 m × 6.6 m is designed with Table 26. Is that right?
quiz.a: No: l<sub>y</sub>/l<sub>x</sub> = 1.83 is fine (≤ 2), so it is two-way; but at 3.6 m × 7.5 m (2.08) it must be designed as one-way and Table 26 does not apply.

beyond: Not for the exam. The coefficients come from yield line and elastic plate solutions; designers now check irregular panels, openings and point loads with finite element plate models. Two-way ribbed (waffle) slabs and post-tensioned slabs carry longer spans. Search for "IS 456 Annex D background" and "waffle slab design".

figure.caption: The 3.496 m × 4.488 m panel of the worked example. The two continuous edges carry the hogging moments and top steel; the corner where both edges are discontinuous gets the full torsion mesh over 0.70 m, the two mixed corners half of it, and the corner between two continuous edges none.
